\right]^{RU} =
B_k^\circ
\bigl(I_d^-(\beta),\alpha\bigr).
\end{equation*}
Consequently, by Lemma~\ref{l:B circ with inss}, we have
\begin{equation*}
f_{2k}(W)=
\mathrm{inss}_{2h}
\left(
B_k^\circ\bigl(I_d^-(\beta),\alpha\bigr)
\right)=
B_k
\bigl(I_d^-(\beta),I_h^+(\alpha)\bigr).
\end{equation*}
Therefore, by the definition of $F_k$, we conclude that
\begin{equation*}
F_k
\bigl(I_d^-(\sigma),I_h^+(\tau)\bigr)
=
\bigl(I_d^-(\beta),I_h^+(\alpha)\bigr),
\end{equation*}
which proves $(E_k)$.

We next assume $(E_{k})$ together with $(D_{k-1})$
to prove $(D_k)$. Suppose that
\begin{equation*}
F_k(\sigma,\tau)=(\alpha,\beta).
\end{equation*}
Let $d$ be the position of $1$ in $\sigma$, and let $h$ be the position
of $k$ in $\tau$. There are unique
$\sigma',\tau'\in\mathfrak{S}_{k-1}$ such that
\begin{equation*}
\sigma=I_d^-(\sigma'),
\qquad
\tau=I_h^+(\tau').
\end{equation*}
Write
\begin{equation*}
F_{k-1}(\sigma',\tau')=(\alpha',\beta').
\end{equation*}
Applying $(E_k)$, we have
\begin{equation*}
\alpha=I_d^-(\beta'),
\qquad
\beta=I_h^+(\alpha').
\end{equation*}

By $(D_{k-1})$,
\begin{equation*}
F_{k-1}
\bigl((\tau')^{RU},(\sigma')^{RU}\bigr)
=
\bigl((\beta')^{RU},(\alpha')^{RU}\bigr).
\end{equation*}
Lemma~\ref{l:ins RU identity} give
\begin{equation*}
\tau^{RU}
=
I_{k+1-h}^-\bigl((\tau')^{RU}\bigr),
\qquad
\sigma^{RU}
=
I_{k+1-d}^+\bigl((\sigma')^{RU}\bigr).
\end{equation*}
Applying $(E_k)$ again, $F_k(\tau^{RU},\sigma^{RU})$ equals
\begin{equation*}
F_k\left(
I_{k+1-h}^-\bigl((\tau')^{RU}\bigr),
I_{k+1-d}^+\bigl((\sigma')^{RU}\bigr)
\right)
=
\left(
I_{k+1-h}^-\bigl((\alpha')^{RU}\bigr),
I_{k+1-d}^+\bigl((\beta')^{RU}\bigr)
\right).
\end{equation*}
Using Lemma~\ref{l:ins RU identity} once more,
\begin{equation*}
I_{k+1-h}^-\bigl((\alpha')^{RU}\bigr)
=\bigr(I_h^+(\alpha')\bigr)^{RU}
=\beta^{RU},
\qquad
I_{k+1-d}^+\bigl((\beta')^{RU}\bigr)
= \bigr(I_d^-(\beta')\bigr)^{RU}
=\alpha^{RU}.
\end{equation*}


Therefore,
\begin{equation*}
F_k(\tau^{RU},\sigma^{RU})
=
(\beta^{RU},\alpha^{RU}),
\end{equation*}
which proves $(D_k)$ and completes the induction.
<!-- end proof-52 -->
<!-- thm-8: body_md -->
\label{t:rank-matrix}
Let $u,w\in\mathfrak{S}_n$. Then
\begin{equation*}
u\leq w
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
r_u(a,b)\geq r_w(a,b)
\end{equation*}
for all $a,b\in[n]$.
<!-- end thm-8 -->
<!-- lem-25: body_md -->
\label{l:rank B}
Let $\alpha,\beta\in\mathfrak S_k$ and
\begin{equation*}
u=B_k(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathfrak B_{2k}.
\end{equation*}
Then, for all $a,b\in[2k]$,
\begin{equation*}
r_u(a,b)
=
r_\alpha\left(
\ceil[\Big]{\frac{a}{2}},
\ceil[\Big]{\frac{b}{2}}
\right)
+
r_\beta\left(
\floor[\Big]{\frac{a}{2}},
\floor[\Big]{\frac{b}{2}}
\right).
\end{equation*}
<!-- end lem-25 -->
<!-- proof-53: body_md -->
Among the first $a$ positions of $u=B_k(\alpha,\beta)$, there are
$\ceil{\tfrac{a}{2}}$ odd positions and
$\floor{\tfrac{a}{2}}$ even positions.

The entries in the odd positions are
\begin{equation*}
2\alpha_1-1,\ldots,
2\alpha_{\ceil{\tfrac{a}{2}}}-1.
\end{equation*}
For each $i$, we know that
\begin{equation*}
2\alpha_i-1\leq b
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\alpha_i\leq \ceil[\Big]{\frac{b}{2}}.
\end{equation*}
Hence the contribution from the odd positions is $r_\alpha\left(
\ceil{\tfrac{a}{2}},
\ceil{\tfrac{b}{2}}
\right)$.


Similarly, the entries in the even positions are
\begin{equation*}
2\beta_1,\ldots,
2\beta_{\floor{\tfrac{a}{2}}}.
\end{equation*}
For each $j$, we know that
\begin{equation*}
2\beta_j\leq b
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\beta_j\leq \floor[\Big]{\frac{b}{2}}.
\end{equation*}
Hence the contribution from the even positions is
$r_\beta\left(
\floor{\tfrac{a}{2}},
\floor{\tfrac{b}{2}}
\right)$.

Adding the two contributions gives
\begin{equation*}
r_u(a,b)
=
r_\alpha\left(
\ceil[\Big]{\frac{a}{2}},
\ceil[\Big]{\frac{b}{2}}
\right)
+
r_\beta\left(
\floor[\Big]{\frac{a}{2}},
\floor[\Big]{\frac{b}{2}}
\right).
\end{equation*}
<!-- end proof-53 -->
<!-- lem-26: body_md -->
\label{l:rank insertion}
Let $w\in\mathfrak S_{k-1}$.

\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
    \item For $d\in[k]$ and $a,b\in[k]$,
    \begin{equation}
    r_{I_d^-(w)}(a,b)
    =
    \begin{cases}
    r_w(a,b-1), & d>a,\\[4pt]
    1+r_w(a-1,b-1), & d\leq a.
    \end{cases}
    \label{eq:rank minimum insertion}
    \end{equation}

    \item For $h\in[k]$, $a\in[k]$, and $b\in[k-1]$,
    \begin{equation}
    r_{I_h^+(w)}(a,b)
    =
    \begin{cases}
    r_w(a,b), & h>a,\\[4pt]
    r_w(a-1,b), & h\leq a.
    \end{cases}
    \label{eq:rank maximum insertion}
    \end{equation}
\end{enumerate}
Here we use the convention $r_w(a,0)=0$.
<!-- end lem-26 -->
<!-- proof-54: body_md -->
For \eqref{eq:rank minimum insertion}, recall that $I_d^-(w)$ is
obtained by increasing every entry of $w$ by $1$ and inserting $1$ in
position $d$. If $d>a$, the inserted $1$ does not occur among the first
$a$ positions, and an entry of $I_d^-(w)$ is at most $b$ precisely when
the corresponding entry of $w$ is at most $b-1$. Hence
\begin{equation*}
r_{I_d^-(w)}(a,b)=r_w(a,b-1).
\end{equation*}
If $d\leq a$, the inserted $1$ contributes one to the rank, while the
remaining $a-1$ entries contribute $r_w(a-1,b-1)$. Thus
\begin{equation*}
r_{I_d^-(w)}(a,b)
=
1+r_w(a-1,b-1).
\end{equation*}

For \eqref{eq:rank maximum insertion}, $I_h^+(w)$ is obtained by
inserting the new maximum $k$ in position $h$. Since $b\leq k-1$, the
inserted entry $k$ does not contribute to the rank. If $h>a$, the first
$a$ entries are unchanged, while if $h\leq a$, only $a-1$ entries of
$w$ occur among the first $a$ positions. Therefore,
\begin{equation*}
r_{I_h^+(w)}(a,b)
=
\begin{cases}
r_w(a,b), & h>a,\\[4pt]
r_w(a-1,b), & h\leq a.
\end{cases}
\end{equation*}
<!-- end proof-54 -->
<!-- lem-27: body_md -->
\label{l:Rk}
Let $\sigma,\tau,\alpha,\beta\in\mathfrak S_k$, and suppose that
\begin{equation*}
F_k(\sigma,\tau)=(\alpha,\beta).
\end{equation*}
Then, for all $a,b\in[k]$ and $0\leq p\leq a$,
\begin{equation}
r_\sigma(a,b)
\geq
r_\alpha\left(
p,
\ceil[\Big]{\frac{b}{2}}
\right)
+
r_\beta\left(
a-p,
\floor[\Big]{\frac{b}{2}}
\right).
\tag{$R_k$}
\end{equation}
<!-- end lem-27 -->
<!-- proof-55: body_md -->
Before we start, we call $a,b,p$ the first, second, third parameter of $(R_k)$. Now, we proceed by induction on $k$. We use the convention
$r_w(0,b)=r_w(a,0)=0$. With this convention, the statement is also
trivial when one of the parameters occurring in the induction
hypothesis is zero. 

For $k=2$, by Algorithm~\ref{keyalg}, the map $F_2$ is the identity map on
$\mathfrak S_2\times\mathfrak S_2$. Thus $\alpha=\sigma$ and
$\beta=\tau$. If $b=1$, then
\begin{equation*}
r_\alpha(p,1)+r_\beta(a-p,0)
=
r_\sigma(p,1)
\leq
r_\sigma(a,1).
\end{equation*}
If $b=2$, then
\begin{equation*}
r_\alpha(p,1)+r_\beta(a-p,1)
\leq
p+(a-p)
=
a
=
r_\sigma(a,2).
\end{equation*}
Hence $(R_2)$ holds.

Now let $k\geq 3$ and assume $(R_{k-1})$. Suppose that
\begin{equation*}
F_k(\sigma,\tau)=(\alpha,\beta).
\end{equation*}
Let $d$ be the position of $1$ in $\sigma$, and let $h$ be the position
of $k$ in $\tau$. Then there exist
$\sigma',\tau'\in\mathfrak S_{k-1}$ such that
\begin{equation*}
\sigma=I_d^-(\sigma'),
\qquad
\tau=I_h^+(\tau').
\end{equation*}
Write
\begin{equation*}
F_{k-1}(\sigma',\tau')=(\alpha',\beta').
\end{equation*}
By $(E_k)$ in Proposition~\ref{p:Ek Dk},
\begin{equation*}
\alpha=I_d^-(\beta'),
\qquad
\beta=I_h^+(\alpha').
\end{equation*}

Fix $a,b\in[k]$ and $0\leq p\leq a$. Define
\begin{equation*}
\delta=\mathbf{1}_{d\leq a},
\qquad
\eta=\mathbf{1}_{d\leq p},
\qquad
\varepsilon=\mathbf{1}_{h\leq a-p}.
\end{equation*}
Since $p\leq a$, we always have $\eta\leq\delta$.

By \eqref{eq:rank minimum insertion} and
\eqref{eq:rank maximum insertion}, we have

\begin{gather}
r_\sigma(a,b)
=
\delta+r_{\sigma'}(a-\delta,b-1),\label{eq:rank function with delta}\\
r_\alpha\left(p,\ceil[\Big]{\frac{b}{2}}\right)
=
\eta+
r_{\beta'}\left(
p-\eta,
\ceil[\Big]{\frac{b}{2}}-1
\right),\label{eq:rank function alpha}\\
r_\beta\left(a-p,\floor[\Big]{\frac{b}{2}}\right)
=
r_{\alpha'}\left(
a-p-\varepsilon,
\floor[\Big]{\frac{b}{2}}
\right).\label{eq:rank function beta}
\end{gather}


Now, set $q=a-p-\varepsilon$.

We first consider the case $(\delta,p,\varepsilon)\neq(1,0,0)$.
Then, we have $0\leq q\leq a-\delta$.
Indeed, $q\geq0$ by the definition of $\varepsilon$, while
$q\leq a-\delta$ is equivalent to $p+\varepsilon\geq\delta$, which
fails only when $(\delta,p,\varepsilon)=(1,0,0)$.

Note that $(a-\delta)-q = (a-\delta)-(a-p-\varepsilon) =p+\varepsilon -\delta$. By the definition of $\delta$, we have \begin{equation*}
a-\delta \leq
\begin{cases}
k - \delta = k -1, &\text{when} \ a = k,\\[4pt]
k-1-\delta \leq k-1, &\text{when} \ a < k. 
\end{cases}
\end{equation*}
We also note that $b-1 \leq k-1$. 
Applying $(R_{k-1})$ with parameters $a-\delta,b-1,q$ and using
\begin{equation*}
\ceil[\Big]{\frac{b-1}{2}}
=
\floor[\Big]{\frac{b}{2}},
\qquad
\floor[\Big]{\frac{b-1}{2}}
=
\ceil[\Big]{\frac{b}{2}}-1,
\end{equation*}
we obtain
\begin{equation*}
r_{\sigma'}(a-\delta,b-1)
\geq{}
r_{\alpha'}\left(
q,
\floor[\Big]{\frac{b}{2}}
\right) +
r_{\beta'}\left(
p+\varepsilon-\delta,
\ceil[\Big]{\frac{b}{2}}-1
\right).
\end{equation*}
Comparing this inequality with \eqref{eq:rank function with delta}, we have
\begin{equation}\label{eq:NW first ineq}
r_\sigma(a,b)
\geq{}
r_{\alpha'}\left(
q,
\floor[\Big]{\frac{b}{2}}
\right)+
\delta+
r_{\beta'}\left(
p+\varepsilon-\delta,
\ceil[\Big]{\frac{b}{2}}-1
\right).
\end{equation}

Next, we claim that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:NW prop claim}
\delta+
r_{\beta'}\left(
p+\varepsilon-\delta,
\ceil[\Big]{\frac{b}{2}}-1
\right)
\geq
\eta+
r_{\beta'}\left(
p-\eta,
\ceil[\Big]{\frac{b}{2}}-1
\right).
\end{equation}
To see this, we first note that $\delta \geq \eta$ by above definition. Then, it remains to compare the other two terms. 
If $p-\eta\leq p+\varepsilon-\delta$, \eqref{eq:NW prop claim} follows from the monotonicity of the rank function in its first argument. Otherwise, we have $p-\eta > p+\varepsilon-\delta$, i.e., $\eta < \delta -\varepsilon$. Hence 
\begin{equation*}
\delta=1,
\qquad
\eta=\varepsilon=0,
\end{equation*}
and the claim~\eqref{eq:NW prop claim} follows from $r_{\beta'}(x+1,y)\leq r_{\beta'}(x,y)+1$ for all (possible) $x$ and $y$. 

Comparing the right-hand-side of \eqref{eq:NW prop claim} with \eqref{eq:rank function alpha} and by \eqref{eq:rank function beta}, we have 
\begin{equation*}
r_\sigma(a,b)
\geq{}
r_{\alpha'}\left(
q,
\floor[\Big]{\frac{b}{2}}
\right)
+
\eta+
r_{\beta'}\left(
p-\eta,
\ceil[\Big]{\frac{b}{2}}-1
\right)
={}
r_\beta\left(
a-p,\floor[\Big]{\frac{b}{2}}
\right)
+
r_\alpha\left(
p,\ceil[\Big]{\frac{b}{2}}
\right).
\end{equation*}

It remains to consider the boundary case $(\delta,p,\varepsilon)=(1,0,0)$.
Since $p=0$, by the definition of $\eta$, we have $\eta=0$. Since $\varepsilon=0$ and $p=0$, we have $h>a$. Therefore, \eqref{eq:rank function with delta} and \eqref{eq:rank function beta} become
\begin{equation*}
r_\sigma(a,b)
=
1+r_{\sigma'}(a-1,b-1)
\end{equation*}
and
\begin{equation*}
r_\beta\left(a,\floor[\Big]{\frac{b}{2}}\right)
=
r_{\alpha'}\left(a,\floor[\Big]{\frac{b}{2}}\right).
\end{equation*}
Indeed, $r_{\alpha'}\left(a,\floor*{\tfrac{b}{2}}\right)$ is well-defined since $h > a$ implies $a \leq k-1$. 
Applying $(R_{k-1})$ 
such that the third parameter equals $a-1$,
we obtain
\begin{equation*}
r_{\sigma'}(a-1,b-1)
\geq
r_{\alpha'}\left(
a-1,\floor[\Big]{\frac{b}{2}}
\right) + r_{\beta'}\left(
0,
\ceil[\Big]{\frac{b}{2}}-1
\right) = r_{\alpha'}\left(
a-1,\floor[\Big]{\frac{b}{2}}
\right).
\end{equation*}
Since increasing the first argument of a rank function by one increases
its value by at most one, we have
\begin{equation*}
1+
r_{\alpha'}\left(
a-1,\floor[\Big]{\frac{b}{2}}
\right)
\geq
r_{\alpha'}\left(
a,\floor[\Big]{\frac{b}{2}}
\right).
\end{equation*}
Hence, by \eqref{eq:rank function with delta}
\begin{equation*}
r_\sigma(a,b)
\geq
r_{\alpha'}\left(
a,\floor[\Big]{\frac{b}{2}}
\right).
\end{equation*}
Since $\beta = I_h^+(\alpha')$ and $h>a$, inserting the maximum entry at position $h$ does not change the rank function. We have 
\begin{equation*}
   r_{\alpha'}\left(
a,\floor[\Big]{\frac{b}{2}}
\right) = r_{I_h^+(\alpha')}\left(
a,\floor[\Big]{\frac{b}{2}}
\right) = r_{\beta}\left(
a,\floor[\Big]{\frac{b}{2}}
\right).
\end{equation*}
Hence, we have 
\begin{equation*}
    r_\sigma(a,b) \geq r_{\beta}\left(
a,\floor[\Big]{\frac{b}{2}}
\right)
\end{equation*}
Since
$r_\alpha\left(
0,\ceil{\tfrac{b}{2}}
\right)=0$, this is precisely $(R_k)$ when $p=0$.

Thus $(R_k)$ holds, completing the induction.
<!-- end proof-55 -->
<!-- cor-14: body_md -->
\label{c:NW quadrant}
Let $\sigma,\tau,\alpha,\beta\in\mathfrak S_k$, and suppose that
\begin{equation*}
F_k(\sigma,\tau)=(\alpha,\beta).
\end{equation*}
Then, for all $a,b\in[k]$,
\begin{equation*}
r_{A_k(\sigma,\tau)}(a,b)
\geq
r_{B_k(\alpha,\beta)}(a,b).
\end{equation*}
<!-- end cor-14 -->
<!-- proof-56: body_md -->
Since $a,b\in[k]$, by the definition of $A_k$,
\begin{equation*}
r_{A_k(\sigma,\tau)}(a,b)=r_\sigma(a,b).
\end{equation*}
Applying $(R_k)$ in Lemma~\ref{l:Rk} with
$p=\ceil{\tfrac{a}{2}}$,
we obtain
\begin{equation*}
r_\sigma(a,b)
\geq{}
r_\alpha\left(
\ceil[\Big]{\frac{a}{2}},
\ceil[\Big]{\frac{b}{2}}
\right)
+
r_\beta\left(
\floor[\Big]{\frac{a}{2}},
\floor[\Big]{\frac{b}{2}}
\right),
\end{equation*}
where we have used
\begin{equation*}
a-\ceil[\Big]{\frac{a}{2}}
=
\floor[\Big]{\frac{a}{2}}.
\end{equation*}
By Lemma~\ref{l:rank B}, the right-hand side is precisely
\begin{equation*}
r_{B_k(\alpha,\beta)}(a,b).
\end{equation*}
Hence
\begin{equation*}
r_{A_k(\sigma,\tau)}(a,b)
\geq
r_{B_k(\alpha,\beta)}(a,b),
\end{equation*}
as desired.
<!-- end proof-56 -->
<!-- lem-28: body_md -->
\label{l:mixed quadrants}
Let $\sigma,\tau,\alpha,\beta\in\mathfrak S_k$, and suppose that
\begin{equation*}
F_k(\sigma,\tau)=(\alpha,\beta).
\end{equation*}
Then
\begin{equation*}
r_{A_k(\sigma,\tau)}(a,b)
\geq
r_{B_k(\alpha,\beta)}(a,b)
\end{equation*}
whenever either $a\leq k<b$ or $b\leq k<a$.
<!-- end lem-28 -->
<!-- proof-57: body_md -->
First suppose that $a\leq k<b$. Since the first $a$ entries of
$A_k(\sigma,\tau)$ all belong to $[k]$, they are all at most $b$.
Therefore, $r_{A_k(\sigma,\tau)}(a,b)=a$.

On the other hand, for any permutation $w$ we have
$r_w(a,b)\leq a$. Hence
\begin{equation*}
r_{A_k(\sigma,\tau)}(a,b)
=
a
\geq
r_{B_k(\alpha,\beta)}(a,b).
\end{equation*}

Now suppose that $b\leq k<a$. Among the first $k$ entries of
$A_k(\sigma,\tau)$, each element of $[k]$ occurs exactly once, while
all entries after position $k$ are greater than $k$. Thus exactly $b$
of the first $a$ entries are at most $b$, and hence
$r_{A_k(\sigma,\tau)}(a,b)=b$.
Since $r_w(a,b)\leq b$ for every permutation $w$, we obtain
\begin{equation*}
r_{A_k(\sigma,\tau)}(a,b)
=
b
\geq
r_{B_k(\alpha,\beta)}(a,b).
\end{equation*}
<!-- end proof-57 -->
<!-- lem-29: body_md -->
\label{l:rank RU}
Let $w\in\mathfrak S_{2k}$. Then, for all $a,b\in[2k]$,
\begin{equation}
r_w(a,b)
=
a+b-2k
+
r_{w^{RU}}(2k-a,2k-b).
\label{eq:rank RU}
\end{equation}
Here we use the convention
$r_w(0,b)=r_w(a,0)=0$.
<!-- end lem-29 -->
<!-- proof-58: body_md -->
Among the $2k$ entries of $w$, exactly $2k-b$ are greater than $b$.
Let $N$ denote the number of such entries occurring among the first
$a$ positions. Then
\begin{equation*}
r_w(a,b)=a-N.
\end{equation*}

Write
$w^{RU}=v_1\cdots v_{2k}$. 
By the definition of $RU$,
$v_j=2k+1-w_{2k+1-j}$
for every $j\in[2k]$.

Now consider an entry $w_i$ of $w$ with $i>a$ and $w_i>b$.
Under $RU$, this entry corresponds to the entry
\begin{equation*}
v_{2k+1-i}=2k+1-w_i
\end{equation*}
of $w^{RU}$. Since $i>a$, we have
\begin{equation*}
2k+1-i\leq 2k-a,
\end{equation*}
and since $w_i>b$, we have
\begin{equation*}
2k+1-w_i\leq 2k-b.
\end{equation*}
Thus, each entry of $w$ greater than $b$ and occurring after position
$a$ corresponds to an entry of $w^{RU}$ among its first $2k-a$
positions whose value is at most $2k-b$.

Conversely, suppose that $v_j$ is among the first $2k-a$ positions of
$w^{RU}$ with $v_j\leq 2k-b$. The corresponding entry of $w$
is
\begin{equation*}
w_{2k+1-j}=2k+1-v_j.
\end{equation*}
Since $j\leq 2k-a$, we have
\begin{equation*}
2k+1-j>a,
\end{equation*}
and since $v_j\leq 2k-b$, we have
\begin{equation*}
2k+1-v_j>b.
\end{equation*}
Therefore, this correspondence is a bijection between the entries of
$w$ greater than $b$ occurring after position $a$ and the entries of
$w^{RU}$ among its first $2k-a$ positions whose values are at most
$2k-b$.

Hence the number of entries of $w$ greater than $b$ occurring after
position $a$ is
\begin{equation*}
r_{w^{RU}}(2k-a,2k-b).
\end{equation*}
Since the total number of entries of $w$ greater than $b$ is $2k-b$,
we obtain
\begin{equation*}
N
=
2k-b-r_{w^{RU}}(2k-a,2k-b).
\end{equation*}
Substituting this into $r_w(a,b)=a-N$ gives
\begin{equation*}
r_w(a,b)=
a+b-2k+r_{w^{RU}}(2k-a,2k-b).
\end{equation*}
<!-- end proof-58 -->
<!-- lem-30: body_md -->
\label{l:SE quadrant}
Let $\sigma,\tau,\alpha,\beta\in\mathfrak S_k$, and suppose that
\begin{equation*}
F_k(\sigma,\tau)=(\alpha,\beta).
\end{equation*}
Then, for all $a,b\in[k+1,2k]$, we have 
\begin{equation*}
r_{A_k(\sigma,\tau)}(a,b)
\geq
r_{B_k(\alpha,\beta)}(a,b).
\end{equation*}
<!-- end lem-30 -->
<!-- proof-59: body_md -->
Fix $a,b\in[k+1,2k]$, and set
\begin{equation*}
\unexpanded{\protect\mathaccentV{bar}}\number\symboldoperators16 a=2k-a,
\qquad
\unexpanded{\protect\mathaccentV{bar}}\number\symboldoperators16 b=2k-b.
\end{equation*}
Then we have $0\leq \unexpanded{\protect\mathaccentV{bar}}\number\symboldoperators16 a,\unexpanded{\protect\mathaccentV{bar}}\number\symboldoperators16 b\leq k-1$.

By Lemma~\ref{l:RU on A B}, we have
\begin{equation*}
A_k(\sigma,\tau)^{RU}
=
A_k(\tau^{RU},\sigma^{RU}), \ \text{and} \
B_k(\alpha,\beta)^{RU}
=
B_k(\beta^{RU},\alpha^{RU}).
\end{equation*}
Moreover, by $(D_k)$ in Proposition~\ref{p:Ek Dk},
\begin{equation*}
F_k(\tau^{RU},\sigma^{RU})
=
(\beta^{RU},\alpha^{RU}).
\end{equation*}

If $\unexpanded{\protect\mathaccentV{bar}}\number\symboldoperators16 a,\unexpanded{\protect\mathaccentV{bar}}\number\symboldoperators16 b\geq 1$, Corollary~\ref{c:NW quadrant} applied to
\begin{equation*}
F_k(\tau^{RU},\sigma^{RU})
=
(\beta^{RU},\alpha^{RU})
\end{equation*}
gives
\begin{equation*}
r_{A_k(\tau^{RU},\sigma^{RU})}(\unexpanded{\protect\mathaccentV{bar}}\number\symboldoperators16 a,\unexpanded{\protect\mathaccentV{bar}}\number\symboldoperators16 b)
\geq
r_{B_k(\beta^{RU},\alpha^{RU})}(\unexpanded{\protect\mathaccentV{bar}}\number\symboldoperators16 a,\unexpanded{\protect\mathaccentV{bar}}\number\symboldoperators16 b).
\end{equation*}

If either $\unexpanded{\protect\mathaccentV{bar}}\number\symboldoperators16 a=0$ or $\unexpanded{\protect\mathaccentV{bar}}\number\symboldoperators16 b=0$, both sides are zero.
Thus, in all cases,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:SE quadrant RU}
r_{A_k(\sigma,\tau)^{RU}}(\unexpanded{\protect\mathaccentV{bar}}\number\symboldoperators16 a,\unexpanded{\protect\mathaccentV{bar}}\number\symboldoperators16 b)
\geq
r_{B_k(\alpha,\beta)^{RU}}(\unexpanded{\protect\mathaccentV{bar}}\number\symboldoperators16 a,\unexpanded{\protect\mathaccentV{bar}}\number\symboldoperators16 b).
\end{equation}

Applying \eqref{eq:rank RU} to $A_k(\sigma,\tau)$, we obtain
\begin{equation*}
r_{A_k(\sigma,\tau)}(a,b)
=
a+b-2k
+
r_{A_k(\sigma,\tau)^{RU}}(\unexpanded{\protect\mathaccentV{bar}}\number\symboldoperators16 a,\unexpanded{\protect\mathaccentV{bar}}\number\symboldoperators16 b).
\end{equation*}
Similarly,
\begin{equation*}
r_{B_k(\alpha,\beta)}(a,b)
=
a+b-2k
+
r_{B_k(\alpha,\beta)^{RU}}(\unexpanded{\protect\mathaccentV{bar}}\number\symboldoperators16 a,\unexpanded{\protect\mathaccentV{bar}}\number\symboldoperators16 b).
\end{equation*}
Therefore, by \eqref{eq:SE quadrant RU}, we have 
\begin{align*}
r_{A_k(\sigma,\tau)}(a,b)
&=
a+b-2k
+
r_{A_k(\sigma,\tau)^{RU}}(\unexpanded{\protect\mathaccentV{bar}}\number\symboldoperators16 a,\unexpanded{\protect\mathaccentV{bar}}\number\symboldoperators16 b)\\
&\geq
a+b-2k
+
r_{B_k(\alpha,\beta)^{RU}}(\unexpanded{\protect\mathaccentV{bar}}\number\symboldoperators16 a,\unexpanded{\protect\mathaccentV{bar}}\number\symboldoperators16 b)\\
&=
r_{B_k(\alpha,\beta)}(a,b).
\end{align*}
This proves the southeast quadrant.
<!-- end proof-59 -->
<!-- cor-15: body_md -->
\label{c:rank comparison even}
Let $\sigma,\tau,\alpha,\beta\in\mathfrak S_k$, and suppose that
\begin{equation*}
F_k(\sigma,\tau)=(\alpha,\beta).
\end{equation*}
Then, for all $a,b\in[2k]$, we have
\begin{equation*}
r_{A_k(\sigma,\tau)}(a,b)
\geq
r_{B_k(\alpha,\beta)}(a,b).
\end{equation*}
<!-- end cor-15 -->
<!-- thm-9: body_md -->
\label{thm:even case}
Let $n=2k$ ($k\geq 2$). Then, for every $w\in\mathfrak A_{2k}$,
\begin{equation*}
w\leq f_{2k}(w)
\end{equation*}
under the Bruhat order.
<!-- end thm-9 -->
<!-- proof-60: body_md -->
This follows immediately from Corollary~\ref{c:rank comparison even}
and Theorem~\ref{t:rank-matrix}.
<!-- end proof-60 -->
<!-- cor-16: body_md -->
\label{c:odd case}
Let $n=2k-1$ ($k\geq 3$). Then, for every $w\in\mathfrak A_{2k-1}$,
\begin{equation*}
w\leq f_{2k-1}(w)
\end{equation*}
under the Bruhat order.
<!-- end cor-16 -->
<!-- proof-61: body_md -->
Let $w\in\mathfrak A_{2k-1}$. Since
$w^{RU}\in\widetilde{\mathfrak A}_{2k-1}$, we have
\begin{equation*}
\mathrm{ins}_{2k}(w^{RU})\in\mathfrak A_{2k}.
\end{equation*}
By the definition of $\widetilde f_{2k-1}$,
\begin{equation*}
\widetilde f_{2k-1}(w^{RU})
=
\left[f_{2k-1}\bigl((w^{RU})^{RU}\bigr)\right]^{RU}
=
f_{2k-1}(w)^{RU}.
\end{equation*}
Since $\mathrm{inss}_{2k}$ inserts $2k$ at the last position, no swapping occurs,
and hence $\mathrm{inss}_{2k}=\mathrm{ins}_{2k}$. Therefore, by the definition of
$f_{2k}$,
\begin{equation*}
f_{2k}\bigl(\mathrm{ins}_{2k}(w^{RU})\bigr)
=
\mathrm{ins}_{2k}\bigl(f_{2k-1}(w)^{RU}\bigr).
\end{equation*}

By Theorem~\ref{thm:even case},
\begin{equation*}
\mathrm{ins}_{2k}(w^{RU})
\leq
\mathrm{ins}_{2k}\bigl(f_{2k-1}(w)^{RU}\bigr).
\end{equation*}
Both permutations have the common last entry $2k$. By the tableau criterion (Theorem~\ref{TabCriterion}), deleting this common last entry gives
\begin{equation*}
w^{RU}\leq f_{2k-1}(w)^{RU}.
\end{equation*}
Since $RU$ preserves the Bruhat order (Proposition~\ref{upside-down reverse}) and is an involution, we conclude
that
\begin{equation*}
w\leq f_{2k-1}(w).
\end{equation*}
<!-- end proof-61 -->
<!-- thm-10: body_md -->
\label{t:Bruhat balance case}
Let $f_n$ be the map defined in Algorithm~\ref{keyalg}. For every $n\geq 4$ and every $w\in\mathfrak A_n$, we have
\begin{equation*}
w\leq f_n(w)
\end{equation*}
under the Bruhat order.
<!-- end thm-10 -->
<!-- proof-62: body_md -->
For even \(n\), the conclusion follows from Theorem~\ref{thm:even case}. For odd \(n\ge5\), it follows from Corollary~\ref{c:odd case}.
<!-- end proof-62 -->
<!-- thm-11: body_md -->
Let $A$ be an $n \times n$ TNN matrix. Then the inequality 
    \begin{equation*}
        \operatorname{per}(A_{[1,h],[1,h]}) \operatorname{per}(A_{[h+1,n],[h+1,n]}) \;\geq\;
    \operatorname{per}(A_{[1,n] \cap 2\mathbb Z, [1,n] \cap 2\mathbb Z})
    \operatorname{per}(A_{[1,n] \smallsetminus 2\mathbb Z, [1,n] \smallsetminus 2\mathbb Z})
    \end{equation*}
    holds when $h = \floor*{\tfrac{n}{2}}$ or $\ceil*{\tfrac{n}{2}}$.
<!-- end thm-11 -->
<!-- prop-15: body_md -->
\label{p:fixed prefix}
Let $k\geq 2$ and $0\leq m\leq k-1$. Let
$\sigma,\tau,\alpha,\beta\in\mathfrak S_k$, such that
\begin{equation*}
F_k(\sigma,\tau)=(\alpha,\beta).
\end{equation*}
If
$\alpha\in\mathfrak S_k^{[\ceil*{\tfrac{m}{2}}]}$
and
$\beta\in\mathfrak S_k^{[\floor*{\tfrac{m}{2}}]}$,
then we have
\begin{equation*}
\sigma\in\mathfrak S_k^{[m]}.
\end{equation*}
<!-- end prop-15 -->
<!-- proof-63: body_md -->
We proceed by induction on $k$. When $k=2$, the case $m=0$ is immediate. For $m=1$, the conclusion follows from the fact that $F_2$ is the identity map on $\mathfrak S_2\times\mathfrak S_2$.

Now let $k\geq 3$, and assume that the proposition holds for $k-1$. Fix $0\leq m\leq k-1$. The case $m=0$ is immediate, so suppose that $m\geq 1$.

Let $d$ be the position of $1$ in $\sigma$, and let $h$ be the position of $k$ in $\tau$. There exist unique $\sigma',\tau'\in\mathfrak S_{k-1}$ such that
\begin{equation*}
\sigma=I_d^-(\sigma'),
\qquad
\tau=I_h^+(\tau').
\end{equation*}
Write
\begin{equation*}
F_{k-1}(\sigma',\tau')=(\alpha',\beta').
\end{equation*}
By $(E_k)$ in Proposition~\ref{p:Ek Dk},
\begin{equation*}
\alpha=I_d^-(\beta'),
\qquad
\beta=I_h^+(\alpha').
\end{equation*}

Since $m\geq 1$, we have $\ceil*{\tfrac{m}{2}}\geq 1$. Thus, $\alpha_1=1$. Since $I_d^-$ inserts the new minimum $1$ at position $d$, it follows that $d=1$. Therefore,
\begin{equation*}
\sigma=I_1^-(\sigma'),
\qquad
\alpha=I_1^-(\beta').
\end{equation*}
Since
\begin{equation*}
\alpha\in\mathfrak S_k^{[\ceil*{\tfrac{m}{2}}]},
\end{equation*}
we obtain
\begin{equation*}
\beta'\in
\mathfrak S_{k-1}^{[\ceil*{\tfrac{m}{2}}-1]}
=
\mathfrak S_{k-1}^{[\floor*{\tfrac{m-1}{2}}]}.
\end{equation*}

We next claim that
\begin{equation*}
h>\floor*{\frac{m}{2}}.
\end{equation*}
To see this, suppose that $h\leq\floor*{\tfrac{m}{2}}$. Since $I_h^+$ inserts the new maximum $k$ in position $h$, we have
$\beta_h=k$.
On the other hand,
$\beta\in\mathfrak S_k^{[\floor*{\tfrac{m}{2}}]}$
implies that $\beta_h=h$. This is impossible, since
\begin{equation*}
h\leq\floor*{\frac{m}{2}}\leq m\leq k-1.
\end{equation*}
Hence we have 
$h>\floor*{\tfrac{m}{2}}$.


It follows that the insertion of $k$ in $I_h^+(\alpha')$ occurs after the first $\floor*{\tfrac{m}{2}}$ positions. Since
\begin{equation*}
\beta=I_h^+(\alpha') \
\text{and} \
\beta\in\mathfrak S_k^{[\floor*{\tfrac{m}{2}}]},
\end{equation*}
we obtain
\begin{equation*}
\alpha'\in
\mathfrak S_{k-1}^{[\floor*{\tfrac{m}{2}}]}
=
\mathfrak S_{k-1}^{[\ceil*{\tfrac{m-1}{2}}]}.
\end{equation*}

Therefore, the induction hypothesis, applied to
\begin{equation*}
F_{k-1}(\sigma',\tau')=(\alpha',\beta')
\end{equation*}
with $m-1$ in place of $m$, gives
\begin{equation*}
\sigma'\in\mathfrak S_{k-1}^{[m-1]}.
\end{equation*}
Finally, since
$\sigma=I_1^-(\sigma')$,
we conclude that
$\sigma\in\mathfrak S_k^{[m]}$.
<!-- end proof-63 -->
<!-- obs-10: body_md -->
\label{o:iota bijection}
The map $\iota_\ell$ restricts to a bijection
\begin{equation*}
\iota_\ell:
\mathfrak S_{2k-\ell}
\longrightarrow
\mathfrak S_{2k}^{[\ell]}.
\end{equation*}
<!-- end obs-10 -->
<!-- proof-64: body_md -->
By definition, every permutation in the image of $\iota_\ell$ fixes the first $\ell$ entries, so
\begin{equation*}
\iota_\ell(\mathfrak S_{2k-\ell})
\subseteq
\mathfrak S_{2k}^{[\ell]}.
\end{equation*}
Conversely, let $v\in\mathfrak S_{2k}^{[\ell]}$. Deleting the initial segment $12\cdots\ell$ and subtracting $\ell$ from each remaining entry gives a unique permutation
$w\in\mathfrak S_{2k-\ell}$
such that
$\iota_\ell(w)=v$.
Hence $\iota_\ell$ is a bijection from $\mathfrak S_{2k-\ell}$ to $\mathfrak S_{2k}^{[\ell]}$.
<!-- end proof-64 -->
<!-- lem-31: body_md -->
\label{l:iota Bruhat}
Let $v,w\in\mathfrak S_{2k-\ell}$. Then
$v\leq w$
if and only if
$\iota_\ell(v)\leq\iota_\ell(w)$.
<!-- end lem-31 -->
<!-- proof-65: body_md -->
For $r\in[2k-\ell]$, let $v_{i,r}$ and $w_{i,r}$ denote the $i$-th entries in the increasing rearrangements of the first $r$ entries of $v$ and $w$, respectively. By the definition of $\iota_\ell$, the increasing rearrangements of the first $\ell+r$ entries of $\iota_\ell(v)$ and $\iota_\ell(w)$ are
\begin{equation*}
1,\ldots,\ell,
v_{1,r}+\ell,\ldots,v_{r,r}+\ell
\end{equation*}
and
\begin{equation*}
1,\ldots,\ell,
w_{1,r}+\ell,\ldots,w_{r,r}+\ell,
\end{equation*}
respectively. Therefore, by the tableau criterion (Theorem~\ref{TabCriterion}),
$v\leq w$
if and only if
$\iota_\ell(v)\leq\iota_\ell(w)$.
<!-- end proof-65 -->
<!-- lem-32: body_md -->
\label{l:iota A}
Let $h\in[n-1]$ with
$h\leq\floor*{\tfrac{n}{2}}$,
and set $k=n-h$, $\ell=n-2h$.
Then 
\begin{equation*}
\iota_\ell\left(\mathfrak A_{n,h}\right)
=
\left\{
A_k(\sigma,\tau)
\mid
\sigma\in\mathfrak S_k^{[\ell]},
\ \tau\in\mathfrak S_k
\right\}.
\end{equation*}
<!-- end lem-32 -->
<!-- proof-66: body_md -->
Let $w\in\mathfrak A_{n,h}$. Since $h=k-\ell$ and $n-h=k$, the first $k-\ell$ entries of $w$ permute $[1,k-\ell]$, while the remaining $k$ entries permute $[k-\ell+1,n]$. Hence, in
\begin{equation*}
\iota_\ell(w)
=
12\cdots\ell\,
(w_1+\ell)\cdots(w_n+\ell),
\end{equation*}
the entries
$(w_1+\ell)\cdots(w_h+\ell)$
permute $[\ell+1,\ell +h] = [\ell+1,k]$. Therefore, the first $k$ entries of $\iota_\ell(w)$ permute $[k]$ and its first $\ell$ entries are $12\cdots\ell$. The last $k$ entries permute $[k+1,2k]$. Therefore, there exist
\begin{equation*}
\sigma\in\mathfrak S_k^{[\ell]},
\qquad
\tau\in\mathfrak S_k
\end{equation*}
such that
\begin{equation*}
\iota_\ell(w)=A_k(\sigma,\tau).
\end{equation*}

Conversely, let $A_k(\sigma,\tau)$ satisfy
\begin{equation*}
\sigma\in\mathfrak S_k^{[\ell]},
\qquad
\tau\in\mathfrak S_k.
\end{equation*}
Since $\sigma$ fixes the first $\ell$ entries, deleting the initial segment $12\cdots\ell$ from $A_k(\sigma,\tau)$ and subtracting $\ell$ from each remaining entry produces a permutation whose first $k-\ell=h$ entries permute $[h]$, while the remaining $k=n-h$ entries permute $[h+1,n]$. Therefore, the resulting permutation lies in $\mathfrak A_{n,h}$.
Hence
$A_k(\sigma,\tau)
\in
\iota_\ell\left(\mathfrak A_{n,h}\right)$,
which proves the result.
<!-- end proof-66 -->
<!-- lem-33: body_md -->
\label{l:iota B}
Let $h\in[n-1]$ with
$h\leq\floor*{\tfrac{n}{2}}$,
and set $k=n-h$, $\ell=n-2h$.
Then
\begin{equation*}
\iota_\ell(\mathfrak B_n)
=
\left\{
B_k(\alpha,\beta)
\mid
\alpha\in\mathfrak S_k^{[\ceil*{\frac{\ell}{2}}]},
\ \beta\in\mathfrak S_k^{[\floor*{\frac{\ell}{2}}]}
\right\}.
\end{equation*}
<!-- end lem-33 -->
<!-- proof-67: body_md -->
Let $u=u_1\cdots u_n\in\mathfrak B_n$. Since $u_i$ and $i$ have the same parity for every $i\in[n]$, the integers $u_i+\ell$ and $i+\ell$ also have the same parity. Together with the fixed initial segment $12\cdots\ell$, this shows that
\begin{equation*}
\iota_\ell(u)\in\mathfrak B_{2k}.
\end{equation*}
Thus, there exist $\alpha,\beta\in\mathfrak S_k$ such that
$\iota_\ell(u)=B_k(\alpha,\beta)$.

Among the first $\ell$ entries of $\iota_\ell(u)$, the odd entries are
\begin{equation*}
1,3,\ldots,2\ceil*{\tfrac{\ell}{2}}-1,
\end{equation*}
while the even entries are
\begin{equation*}
2,4,\ldots,2\floor*{\tfrac{\ell}{2}}.
\end{equation*}
By the definition of $B_k(\alpha,\beta)$, it follows that
\begin{equation*}
\alpha\in\mathfrak S_k^{[\ceil*{\frac{\ell}{2}}]},
\qquad
\beta\in\mathfrak S_k^{[\floor*{\frac{\ell}{2}}]}.
\end{equation*}
Hence
\begin{equation*}
\iota_\ell(\mathfrak B_n)
\subseteq
\left\{
B_k(\alpha,\beta)
\mid
\alpha\in\mathfrak S_k^{[\ceil*{\ell/2}]},
\ \beta\in\mathfrak S_k^{[\floor*{\ell/2}]}
\right\}.
\end{equation*}

Conversely, let
$B_k(\alpha,\beta)$
satisfy
\begin{equation*}
\alpha\in\mathfrak S_k^{[\ceil*{\frac{\ell}{2}}]},
\qquad
\beta\in\mathfrak S_k^{[\floor*{\frac{\ell}{2}}]}.
\end{equation*}
Then the first $\ell$ entries of $B_k(\alpha,\beta)$ are $12\cdots\ell$. Deleting these entries and subtracting $\ell$ from every remaining entry produces a permutation $u\in\mathfrak S_n$. Since both the positions and the corresponding values are shifted by $\ell$, their parities continue to agree. Therefore,
\begin{equation*}
u\in\mathfrak B_n.
\end{equation*}
By construction,
\begin{equation*}
\iota_\ell(u)=B_k(\alpha,\beta),
\end{equation*}
which proves the reverse inclusion.
<!-- end proof-67 -->
<!-- cor-17: body_md -->
\label{c:embedded inverse}
Let $h\in[n-1]$ with
$h\leq\floor*{\frac{n}{2}}$,
and set $k=n-h$, $\ell=n-2h$.
Then
\begin{equation*}
f_{2k}^{-1}\left(\iota_\ell(\mathfrak B_n)\right)
\subseteq
\iota_\ell\left(\mathfrak A_{n,h}\right).
\end{equation*}
<!-- end cor-17 -->
<!-- proof-68: body_md -->
Let $u\in\mathfrak B_n$. By Lemma~\ref{l:iota B}, there exist
\begin{equation*}
\alpha\in\mathfrak S_k^{[\ceil*{\frac{\ell}{2}}]},
\qquad
\beta\in\mathfrak S_k^{[\floor*{\frac{\ell}{2}}]}
\end{equation*}
such that
$\iota_\ell(u)=B_k(\alpha,\beta)$.
Write
\begin{equation*}
f_{2k}^{-1}\left(\iota_\ell(u)\right)
=
A_k(\sigma,\tau).
\end{equation*}
By the definition of $F_k$, we have
\begin{equation*}
F_k(\sigma,\tau)=(\alpha,\beta).
\end{equation*}
Therefore, Proposition~\ref{p:fixed prefix} gives
\begin{equation*}
\sigma\in\mathfrak S_k^{[\ell]}.
\end{equation*}
By Lemma~\ref{l:iota A}, it follows that
\begin{equation*}
A_k(\sigma,\tau)
\in
\iota_\ell\left(\mathfrak A_{n,h}\right).
\end{equation*}
Hence
\begin{equation*}
f_{2k}^{-1}\left(\iota_\ell(u)\right)
\in
\iota_\ell\left(\mathfrak A_{n,h}\right),
\end{equation*}
which proves the result.
<!-- end proof-68 -->
<!-- lem-34: body_md -->
\label{l:g injective}
Let $h\in[n-1]$ with
$h\leq\floor*{\frac{n}{2}}$.
Then the map
\begin{equation*}
g_{n,h}:\mathfrak B_n\to\mathfrak A_{n,h}
\end{equation*}
is injective.
<!-- end lem-34 -->
<!-- proof-69: body_md -->
We prove it by the definition of an injection. 
Let $u,v\in\mathfrak B_n$, and suppose that
\begin{equation*}
g_{n,h}(u)=g_{n,h}(v).
\end{equation*}
By the definition of $g_{n,h}$,
\begin{equation*}
\iota_\ell^{-1}
\left(
f_{2k}^{-1}\left(\iota_\ell(u)\right)
\right)
=
\iota_\ell^{-1}
\left(
f_{2k}^{-1}\left(\iota_\ell(v)\right)
\right).
\end{equation*}
Since $\iota_\ell$ is a bijection onto $\mathfrak S_{2k}^{[\ell]}$, it follows that
\begin{equation*}
f_{2k}^{-1}\left(\iota_\ell(u)\right)
=
f_{2k}^{-1}\left(\iota_\ell(v)\right).
\end{equation*}
Since $f_{2k}$ is a bijection, we obtain
\begin{equation*}
\iota_\ell(u)=\iota_\ell(v).
\end{equation*}
Finally, since $\iota_\ell$ is injective, we conclude that
\begin{equation*}
u=v.
\end{equation*}
Hence $g_{n,h}$ is injective.
<!-- end proof-69 -->
<!-- lem-35: body_md -->
\label{l:g Bruhat}
Let $h\in[n-1]$ with
$h\leq\floor*{\frac{n}{2}}$.
Then, for every $u\in\mathfrak B_n$, we have
\begin{equation*}
g_{n,h}(u)\leq u
\end{equation*}
under the Bruhat order.
<!-- end lem-35 -->
<!-- proof-70: body_md -->
Set
\begin{equation*}
k=n-h,
\qquad
\ell=n-2h.
\end{equation*}
Let $u\in\mathfrak B_n$, and write
\begin{equation*}
v=f_{2k}^{-1}\left(\iota_\ell(u)\right).
\end{equation*}
By the definition of $g_{n,h}$,
\begin{equation*}
v=\iota_\ell\left(g_{n,h}(u)\right).
\end{equation*}
Since $v\in\mathfrak A_{2k}$, Theorem~\ref{t:Bruhat balance case} gives
\begin{equation*}
v\leq f_{2k}(v)=\iota_\ell(u).
\end{equation*}
Hence
\begin{equation*}
\iota_\ell\left(g_{n,h}(u)\right)
\leq
\iota_\ell(u).
\end{equation*}
Since $n = 2k-\ell$, applying Lemma~\ref{l:iota Bruhat}, we immediately obtain 
\begin{equation*}
    g_{n,h}(u)
\leq
u,
\end{equation*}
as desired.
<!-- end proof-70 -->
<!-- lem-36: body_md -->
\label{l:RU A general}
Let $h\in[n-1]$. Then the map $RU$ restricts to a bijection
\begin{equation*}
\mathfrak A_{n,h}
\longrightarrow
\mathfrak A_{n,n-h}.
\end{equation*}
<!-- end lem-36 -->
<!-- proof-71: body_md -->
Let $w=w_1\cdots w_n\in\mathfrak A_{n,h}$. Then we have 
\begin{equation*}
\{w_1,\ldots,w_h\}=[h], 
\ \text{and} \
\{w_{h+1},\ldots,w_n\}=[h+1,n].
\end{equation*}
Write
\begin{equation*}
w^{RU}
=
(n+1-w_n)\cdots(n+1-w_1).
\end{equation*}
The first $n-h$ entries of $w^{RU}$ are obtained from
\begin{equation*}
w_{h+1},\ldots,w_n
\end{equation*}
by reversing their order and replacing each entry $x$ by $n+1-x$. Since
\begin{equation*}
\{w_{h+1},\ldots,w_n\}=[h+1,n],
\end{equation*}
these entries permute $[n-h]$. Similarly, the last $h$ entries of $w^{RU}$ permute
$[n-h+1,n]$.
Therefore,
\begin{equation*}
w^{RU}\in\mathfrak A_{n,n-h}.
\end{equation*}

Since $RU$ is an involution, the reverse inclusion follows in the same way. Hence $RU$ restricts to a bijection between $\mathfrak A_{n,h}$ and $\mathfrak A_{n,n-h}$.
<!-- end proof-71 -->
<!-- prop-16: body_md -->
\label{p:g general}
Let $h\in[n-1]$. Then the map
\begin{equation*}
g_{n,h}:\mathfrak B_n\to\mathfrak A_{n,h}
\end{equation*}
is injective. Moreover, for every $u\in\mathfrak B_n$, we have
\begin{equation*}
g_{n,h}(u)\leq u
\end{equation*}
under the Bruhat order.
<!-- end prop-16 -->
<!-- proof-72: body_md -->
If
$h\leq\floor*{\frac{n}{2}}$,
the result follows from Lemmas~\ref{l:g injective} and~\ref{l:g Bruhat}.

Now suppose that
$h>\floor*{\frac{n}{2}}$.
Then $n-h\leq\floor*{\frac{n}{2}}$, so $g_{n,n-h}$ is injective. Since $RU$ is an involution on $\mathfrak B_n$ and on $\mathfrak S_n$, the definition
\begin{equation*}
g_{n,h}(u)
=
\left(g_{n,n-h}\left(u^{RU}\right)\right)^{RU}
\end{equation*}
immediately implies that $g_{n,h}$ is injective.

Furthermore, by Lemma~\ref{l:g Bruhat},
\begin{equation*}
g_{n,n-h}\left(u^{RU}\right)
\leq
u^{RU}.
\end{equation*}
Since $RU$ preserves the Bruhat order, applying $RU$ to both sides gives
\begin{equation*}
\left(g_{n,n-h}\left(u^{RU}\right)\right)^{RU}
\leq
u.
\end{equation*}
By the definition of $g_{n,h}$, this is
$g_{n,h}(u)\leq u$.
Hence the result holds for all $h\in[n-1]$.
<!-- end proof-72 -->
<!-- thm-12: body_md -->
\label{t:general h TNN}
Let $A$ be an $n\times n$ TNN matrix. Then, for every $h\in[n-1]$,
\begin{equation*}
\operatorname{per}(A_{[1,h],[1,h]})
\operatorname{per}(A_{[h+1,n],[h+1,n]})
\geq
\operatorname{per}(A_{[1,n]\cap 2\mathbb Z,[1,n]\cap 2\mathbb Z})
\operatorname{per}(A_{[1,n]\setminus 2\mathbb Z,[1,n]\setminus 2\mathbb Z}).
\end{equation*}
<!-- end thm-12 -->
<!-- proof-73: body_md -->
For $w\in\mathfrak S_n$, write
\begin{equation*}
x_w=x_{1,w_1}\cdots x_{n,w_n}.
\end{equation*}
Since $g_{n,h}:\mathfrak B_n\to\mathfrak A_{n,h}$ is injective, we have
\begin{equation*}
\sum_{w\in\mathfrak A_{n,h}}x_w
-
\sum_{u\in\mathfrak B_n}x_u
=
\sum_{u\in\mathfrak B_n}
\left(x_{g_{n,h}(u)}-x_u\right)
\quad+
\sum_{w\in\mathfrak A_{n,h}\setminus g_{n,h}(\mathfrak B_n)}
x_w.
\end{equation*}
By Proposition~\ref{p:g general}, we have
$g_{n,h}(u)\leq u$
for every $u\in\mathfrak B_n$. Hence, by Theorem~\ref{pairing test}, each polynomial
$x_{g_{n,h}(u)}-x_u$
is TNN. The remaining monomials are nonnegative on every TNN matrix. Therefore, the entire difference is nonnegative on every TNN matrix, which proves the result.
<!-- end proof-73 -->
<!-- conj-1: body_md -->
Let $A$ be the antiadjacency matrix of an $n$-element unit interval order. Define sets 
    \begin{equation*}
    I= [1,n]_0^3, \quad J = [1,n]_1^3, \quad K = [1,n]_2^3. 
    \end{equation*} 
    Then, for all $1\leq h_1 < h_2 \leq n$, we have 
    \begin{equation*}
        \operatorname{per}(A_{[1,h_1],[1,h_1]}) \operatorname{per}(A_{[h_1,h_2],[h_1,h_2]}) \operatorname{per}(A_{[h_2,n],[h_2,n]}) \geq \operatorname{per}(A_{I,I}) \operatorname{per}(A_{J,J}) \operatorname{per}(A_{K,K}). 
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end conj-1 -->
<!-- prob-1: body_md -->
What kind of TNN matrices satisfy the inequality in Theorem~\ref{t:maintwo}?
<!-- end prob-1 -->
<!-- prob-2: body_md -->
Determine whether the inequalities in Section~\ref{s:A gen on J},
involving products of permanents indexed by residue classes modulo
$s$, admit analogs for arbitrary totally nonnegative matrices.
<!-- end prob-2 -->
<!-- prob-3: body_md -->
Decide which sets $L,K \subseteq [n]$ satisfy 

\begin{equation*}
\operatorname{per}(A_{L,L})\operatorname{per}(A_{\overline{L},\overline{L}}) \geq \operatorname{per}(A_{K,K})\operatorname{per}(A_{\overline{K},\overline{K}})
    \end{equation*} and \begin{equation*}
\det(A_{L,L})\det(A_{\overline{L},\overline{L}}) \leq \det(A_{K,K})\det(A_{\overline{K},\overline{K}})
    \end{equation*} for all TNN matrices.
<!-- end prob-3 -->
<!-- prob-4: body_md -->
Investigate the order-theoretic structure of the maps $f_n$ and
$g_{n,h}$. In particular, determine whether they admit a uniform
description, whether they preserve Bruhat order, and describe the
Bruhat intervals determined by $w$ and its image under these maps.
<!-- end prob-4 -->
